title: How Your Credit Score Really Works

beats.say: Here's something that surprises most people in Britain. There isn't one credit score. There are several. And when you apply for a loan, the lender usually doesn't even look at the number you see in your app.
So what actually decides whether you get a credit card, a phone contract or a mortgage? Let's break down how credit really works in the UK.
Part one. The three agencies.
In the UK, there are three main credit reference agencies. Experian, Equifax and TransUnion. Each one keeps its own file on you, and they don't always have the same information.

And each one gives you a score on its own scale. Experian's now goes up to one thousand two hundred and fifty. Equifax's goes up to one thousand. TransUnion's goes up to seven hundred and ten. So you can't compare them directly.

Experian changed its scale in late twenty twenty five, from nine hundred and ninety nine to twelve hundred and fifty. Millions of people saw their score change overnight, even though nothing about their finances had changed.

vis.text: Your score changed. Your finances didn't.

beats.say: Part two. The number isn't the point.

Here's the big secret. The score you see is mainly a guide, to help you understand your file. Lenders don't usually use it. They look at the information in your credit report, and run it through their own scoring system.
Lenders also look at information you give them, like your income, your job and your outgoings, and some check your bank account data to see how you manage money.

vis.text: Lenders look at your income and spending too.

beats.say: That's why two lenders can make different decisions about the same person. One might say yes, and another no, because they're looking for different kinds of customers.
Part three. What's in your report.

So what's in your credit report? Your credit accounts, like cards, loans, mortgages and phone contracts. Whether you've paid on time. How much credit you're using. And records like county court judgments and bankruptcies.
Payment history is one of the most important parts. Late or missed payments can stay on your file for six years.

vis.text: Missed payments can stay for six years.

beats.say: Other things that can harm your file include defaults, when an account is closed because you didn't pay, county court judgments, and insolvencies like bankruptcy. These usually stay for six years too.
Being on the electoral roll at your address also helps, because lenders use it to confirm who you are and where you live.
Part four. Things that might surprise you.

Having no credit history can be a problem too. If you've never borrowed, lenders have nothing to judge you on. So someone with a long record of paying on time may look safer than someone who's never borrowed at all.
Some people build a history by using a credit card for small regular purchases, like fuel, and paying it off in full every month. That shows lenders you can handle credit responsibly.

vis.text: Small spending, paid off in full, builds history.

beats.say: Using a big share of your credit limit can count against you. A common rule of thumb is to try to keep your balances below about thirty percent of your limits.

Applying for lots of credit in a short time can also look bad. Each full application usually leaves a hard search on your file. But checking your own score, or using eligibility checkers, normally uses a soft search, which lenders don't see.
And if you have a joint account or loan with someone, your files can become financially linked. Their record could affect your applications.

vis.text: Joint finances can link your files.

beats.say: If you split up with someone you had joint finances with, you can ask the credit agencies to remove the financial link once you no longer share any accounts.

vis.text: You can ask to remove an old financial link.

beats.say: Part five. How to improve your chances.
So, what actually helps? None of this is magic, and there are no instant fixes. But these habits are what lenders like to see.

vis.title: Habits lenders like
items: Don't apply for lots at once

beats.say: Some services now let you add things like rent payments or regular bills to your credit file, which can help people with thin files show they pay reliably.
And check your report with all three agencies. You have a legal right to see your report for free. If something's wrong, you can ask for it to be corrected.
Also watch for signs of identity fraud, like accounts you don't recognise. Fraudsters sometimes open credit in other people's names, which can damage their files.

vis.text: Accounts you don't recognise? Check for fraud.

beats.say: So your credit score is useful as a guide. But don't obsess over the number. Focus on what's behind it. A clean, accurate record of paying what you owe, on time.

vis.text: Focus on the record, not the number.
